chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Valuation Matters to You

lessons.title: Price, Value and Worth: Why a Business Has No Single Correct Number

children.text: Two competent people can look at the same company, on the same day, with the same accounts in front of them, and land on numbers that differ by two times or more. Neither of them is bad at arithmetic. They are answering different questions, and the words they use hide that fact.

body.text: Price is what someone paid. Value is what a considered estimate says a business is worth. Worth is what it is to one particular buyer with particular plans. Most valuation arguments are three people using one word for three different things.

children.text: Three Words People Use Interchangeably

cells: Price
The amount actually agreed in a real transaction
A buyer and a seller, on one particular day
Hindustan Unilever paying ₹2,670 crore for 90.5% of Minimalist
Value
An estimate of economic worth, built from cash flows, peer multiples or assets
A valuer, analyst or investor doing the analysis
A DCF concluding that a company is worth ₹240 crore
Worth
What the business is worth to one specific owner, given what they can do with it
The particular buyer, based on their own plans
A rival logistics firm that can shut a duplicate warehouse after buying you

children.text: The valuation profession has language for this.
Fair value
is the price between typical market participants.
Participant specific value
is the value to one identified buyer, synergies included. The gap between the two is exactly why acquirers pay more than investors do.

markDefs.definition: The price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants at the valuation date. It deliberately ignores any one buyer's special advantages.
The value of a business to one identified buyer or owner, including advantages such as synergies that other buyers would not enjoy. Defined in ICAI Valuation Standard 102.

children.text: The Same Business, Four Different Numbers
Nandi Logistics Private Limited is a fictional Hosur company running trucks and two warehouses for auto component makers. Its FY26 numbers are settled and nobody disputes them.

stats.label: EBITDA
stats.context: Operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation

stats.label: Net assets
stats.context: Trucks, warehouses and working capital, net of debt

children.text: Four parties look at Nandi in the same week.
A private equity fund.
It buys the business as it stands and needs an exit in five years. Sector deals are happening at about 8 times EBITDA, so 8 × ₹50 crore = ₹400 crore.
A larger logistics company.
It already has a Hosur depot, so after the merger it can remove ₹10 crore of duplicated costs every year. Its EBITDA becomes ₹60 crore, so 8 × ₹60 crore = ₹480 crore.
A minority investor.
It wants 10% with no board control and no route to sell quickly. Its starting point is 10% of ₹400 crore, which is ₹40 crore, before discounts.
A liquidator.
If the business shuts down and the trucks and warehouses are sold in a hurry, realisations come to roughly ₹110 crore after paying dues.

body.title: Nandi Logistics: value of 100% of the company to different parties

body.text: Nobody changed a single truck. The business is identical in all four cases. What differs is who owns it, what they can do with it, and how quickly they might need their money back. Value is not a property of the company alone.

body.title: Price the synergy
body.prompt: On closer work, the strategic buyer finds it can remove ₹15 crore of duplicated costs a year instead of ₹10 crore. At the same 8 times EBITDA, what is Nandi now worth to that buyer, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹50 crore + ₹15 crore = ₹65 crore of EBITDA after synergies. 8 × ₹65 crore = ₹520 crore. Every rupee of annual synergy added ₹8 of value here, which is why acquirers argue hard about synergies and sellers argue for a share of them.

columns.label: Financial buyer (PE fund)
points: Values the business roughly as it runs today
No operations to merge, so no cost synergies
Needs an exit in four to six years, so the exit multiple matters more than anything
Usually pays with cash raised from the fund and debt

columns.label: Strategic buyer (larger logistics firm)
points: Values the business as part of its own network
Can remove duplicated depots, staff and back office costs
May hold the business permanently, so exit timing is not a constraint
Often pays partly in its own shares, and may hold back an earnout

children.text: Control Has a Price, and So Does Being Stuck
The minority investor cannot simply pay 10% of ₹400 crore. Two adjustments usually apply, and both are judgment calls a valuer must justify. A
discount for lack of control
reflects that the holder cannot decide dividends, hiring or a sale. A
discount for lack of marketability
reflects that there is no exchange on which to sell an unlisted share.

markDefs.definition: A reduction applied to a minority stake because the holder cannot appoint management, set dividend policy or force a sale. The mirror image of a control premium.
A reduction applied because shares in an unlisted company cannot be sold quickly at a reliable price. There is no exchange to sell them on.

body.caption: DLOC is the discount for lack of control and DLOM the discount for lack of marketability

body.title: Show me the discount maths for Nandi

children.text: Take the PE fund's ₹400 crore as the value of 100% of the equity, and assume the valuer supports a 15% discount for lack of control and a 20% discount for lack of marketability.
Pro-rata value of 10%: ₹400 crore × 10% = ₹40 crore
After the 15% control discount: ₹40 crore × 0.85 = ₹34 crore
After the 20% marketability discount: ₹34 crore × 0.80 = ₹27.2 crore
The two discounts together take about 32% off the pro-rata figure, not 35%, because the second applies to what is left after the first. Multiply the discounts, never add them.

content.text: Discount percentages are the softest part of any valuation report and the easiest to argue about. If a report applies them, ask what evidence supports the size chosen. "Standard practice" is not evidence.

children.text: Turn the same idea around and you get the control premium. A buyer taking over a whole company pays more per share than a buyer of a few shares, because only the first one gets to run the business.
Listed Markets Publish a New Price Every Second
For a listed company you never have to guess the price. You do have to remember that the price is a poll of whoever traded today, not a measurement of the business.

body.title: Paytm: one business, wildly different prices

events.title: IPO at ₹2,150 per share
events.description: One 97 Communications raised about ₹18,300 crore, then among the largest Indian IPOs ever. Bankers set the price using valuation work and investor demand.

events.title: Listing day closes about 27% below the issue price
events.description: The market rejected the pricing within hours. Roughly ₹40,000 crore of investor wealth was erased on day one.

events.title: Falls to around ₹310, roughly 86% below the issue price
events.description: Pre-IPO investor lock-ins expired and early backers such as SoftBank sold. Selling pressure, not a single day of operations, drove much of the fall.

events.title: Regulatory action on Paytm Payments Bank
events.description: The RBI barred the associated payments bank from taking fresh deposits, and the share price moved again on news about the business rather than on any valuation report.

children.text: The company on the day of the low was not 86% worse than on listing day. Sentiment, lock-in expiries and fund flows moved the price far more than anything inside the business moved in that window.
Sometimes the Rulebook Sets the Price

In listed markets, some prices are not negotiated at all. Under the SEBI Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers Regulations, 2011, an acquirer crossing 25% of voting rights or acquiring control must make an open offer to public shareholders for at least another 26%. The minimum offer price comes from a formula: the highest of the negotiated deal price, the acquirer's own purchases in the preceding periods and the 60 trading day volume weighted average market price before the announcement.

body.label: Adani group's open offer for NDTV, November 2022
body.context: The formula price was anchored to market prices before the announcement months earlier. By the time the offer opened, NDTV was trading around ₹382 on the BSE, about 30% above the offer price, so shareholders wanting to exit could simply sell on the exchange instead. The offer was undersubscribed.

body.title: Offer price below market price
body.question: You hold 500 NDTV shares in November 2022 and want to sell. The open offer is at ₹294 per share and the stock is trading around ₹382 on the exchange. What does the gap tell you?
options: The open offer price is the true value, so the market price must be wrong
The open offer price is a regulatory floor derived from past prices, so it can sit well below today's market price
Shareholders are legally required to tender into the open offer
The acquirer must raise the open offer price to match the market price
body.explanation: The SAST formula looks backwards at past traded and negotiated prices to protect shareholders from being lowballed relative to history. It says nothing about value today. When the market has moved above the formula price, selling on the exchange is simply the better exit, and no shareholder is obliged to tender.

children.text: So Which Number Is Correct?
None of them, until you say what the valuation is for. The purpose decides whose rules apply and what "correct" even means.

cells: A negotiated sale of a private company
The buyer and the seller, each advised
Whatever both sides sign, informed by their own valuations
Issuing shares to a non-resident investor
FEMA pricing rules, supported by a valuation report from a qualified valuer
The issue price must not be below the fair value arrived at in that report
Granting ESOPs in an unlisted company
Income tax rules on the fair market value of unlisted shares, using a merchant banker's report
The value as at the date the tax rules specify, not the latest round price
Crossing 25% in a listed company
The SEBI takeover formula
A minimum floor price, which the market may well exceed
Reporting an acquired business in the accounts
Accounting standards on fair value
An estimate that the auditor can support with evidence

body.title: Two offers on the table
body.scenario: You own 100% of Nandi Logistics. The PE fund offers ₹400 crore, all cash, closing in 90 days. The strategic buyer offers ₹480 crore: half in cash at closing, half in its own unlisted shares, plus ₹40 crore of the total held back as an earnout payable only if Nandi's EBITDA grows 20% over the next two years.
body.prompt: Which offer is worth more to you? Set out how you would compare them.
body.modelAnswer:
The ₹480 crore headline is not comparable to ₹400 crore of cash until you adjust it.
1. Split the consideration by certainty. Cash at closing is certain. The earnout is a bet on a growth target you may not control after selling, so value it at what you honestly think the odds are, not at face value.
2. Value the buyer's unlisted shares carefully. They carry the same lack of marketability problem covered in this lesson, and you may not be able to sell them for years.
3. Ask what happens to your team and to you. Strategic buyers merge operations, which is exactly where their ₹10 crore of synergies comes from. If you are to stay on, what is the role and for how long?
4. Check the tax and structure of each offer, since cash, shares and earnouts are not taxed identically.
5. Ask why the strategic buyer is paying more. If the extra ₹80 crore is synergy the buyer gets to keep after paying you, the negotiation is about how that ₹80 crore is shared.

body.title: Name the premium
body.textWithBlank: The extra amount a buyer pays per share for the ability to run the company as it wishes is called a control ___.
body.explanation: A control premium is the flip side of the discount for lack of control. The same equity is worth more per share to someone who can decide dividends, management and an eventual sale.

body.title: Questions that settle a valuation argument
steps: Are we talking about a price someone paid or an estimate of value?
Value to whom: a typical market participant, or this specific buyer with synergies?
What size stake, and does it carry control?
Is the stake liquid, and if not, what discount has been applied and on what evidence?
As at what date, and what has changed since?
Which rulebook applies for this purpose: a negotiation, FEMA, tax, SEBI or accounting?

body.label: Screener.in: One 97 Communications (Paytm)
body.description: Look at the price chart alongside the quarterly numbers. Ask yourself how much of the price movement the business results actually explain.

cards.definition: The amount actually agreed in a transaction on a particular day.
An estimate of economic worth based on analysis, not on what anyone paid.
The value of a business to one identified buyer, including synergies only that buyer enjoys.
Cost savings or extra revenue available only after two businesses combine.
The extra paid per share for the power to direct the company.
A reduction applied because the shares cannot be sold quickly at a reliable price.
A mandatory offer to public shareholders when an acquirer crosses 25% of voting rights or acquires control of a listed company.

points: Price is what was paid, value is an estimate, and worth depends on who the buyer is. Say which one you mean.
A strategic buyer with synergies can rationally pay more than a financial buyer for the same business, and Nandi Logistics was worth ₹110 crore to ₹520 crore depending on the party.
Minority stakes in unlisted companies carry discounts for lack of control and lack of marketability. Multiply the discounts, never add them.
Listed prices move on sentiment and fund flows. Paytm fell about 86% below its issue price within a year without the business changing that much.
Some prices are set by rulebooks, such as the SEBI takeover formula that produced NDTV's ₹294 open offer price while the market sat around ₹382.
There is no single correct number until you state the purpose, the date, the stake and the buyer.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Nandi Logistics is fictional. Figures for real companies are drawn from public reports at the time of the events described, and regulatory requirements are summarised in outline only. For any actual transaction, take advice from a qualified valuer and legal counsel.
